challenge: How might science communicators benefit from a free design thinking workshop?
framing: Investigate whether, how and for whom a free design thinking workshop could benefit science communicators, including perceived value, capability, practice change, opportunity costs and unintended effects. Treat “benefit” and “participation” as open questions rather than predefined outcomes.
assumptions: UNRESOLVED QUESTIONS: What does “science communicator” include—professional staff, freelancers, researchers, educators, journalists, community practitioners or volunteers?
UNRESOLVED QUESTIONS: Which geographies, languages, cultural contexts and institutional settings should the research cover?
UNRESOLVED QUESTIONS: What does “young” mean, if age is relevant to the challenge?
UNRESOLVED QUESTIONS: Does “free” mean no registration fee, or also no costs for time, travel, equipment, childcare and lost work?
UNRESOLVED QUESTIONS: What counts as “benefit”—confidence, skills, collaboration, inclusion, audience outcomes, organisational change, wellbeing, income or something else?
UNRESOLVED QUESTIONS: Does “participation” mean registration, attendance, active contribution, completion, later application or sustained involvement?
UNRESOLVED QUESTIONS: Is the workshop intended for individuals, teams, organisations or wider science-communication communities?
UNRESOLVED QUESTIONS: What duration, delivery mode, facilitation model and design-thinking curriculum are under consideration?
UNRESOLVED QUESTIONS: What comparison would make benefit interpretable—no workshop, another training format, paid provision or usual practice?
UNRESOLVED QUESTIONS: Over what timeframe should outcomes and unintended consequences be assessed?

cards.title: Time and Funding Constrain Outreach
cards.takeaway: Outreach participants generally value the activity, but time and funding remain common practical barriers.
cards.finding: In a survey of 530 individuals involved in academic science outreach, 84% reported lack of time and 49% lack of funding as barriers. Among 42 nonparticipants, 67% cited time and 69% funding, while most respondents still viewed outreach favourably.
cards.context: Academic science-outreach participants surveyed; geography and study period not reported.
cards.qualityReason: Large survey with explicit denominators and separate reporting for nonparticipants.
cards.limitation: Self-reported survey responses cannot establish whether these barriers caused nonparticipation or whether findings generalise to professional science communicators.
cards.connection: A workshop may be attractive yet difficult to attend when communicators face similar time and resource pressures.
cards.transferCaution: Respondents were predominantly academic outreach participants, not necessarily employed science communicators or workshop seekers.
cards.discussionQuestion: Which constraints most affect science communicators’ ability to attend or apply workshop learning?

cards.title: Boot Camp Gains Persisted at Two Years
cards.takeaway: A three-day boot camp was associated with higher self-rated communication skills immediately and two years later, though follow-up participation was lower.
cards.finding: Among Science Communication Boot Camp participants, all surveyed skill and attitude measures increased from preworkshop to one week after training; two-year mean scores remained higher than baseline. The two-year follow-up response rate was 45%, and behavioural change was self-reported rather than independently observed.
cards.context: Three-day Science Communication Boot Camp participants; setting and study period not reported in the extract; surveys occurred preworkshop, one week postworkshop, and two years later.
cards.qualityReason: Uses repeated surveys across immediate and two-year timepoints and reports response rates, but no comparison group is described.
cards.limitation: Measures are largely self-reported, follow-up response was 45%, and the extract does not establish that training caused later behaviour or skill gains.
cards.connection: A free design-thinking workshop might similarly produce short-term confidence gains, with longer-term value depending on whether participants apply the methods in practice.
cards.transferCaution: The programme was a three-day science-communication boot camp, not a free design-thinking workshop, and participants may have been especially motivated.
cards.discussionQuestion: Which workshop outcomes should be measured immediately, and which would only become visible after participants return to work?

cards.title: Recognition and time constrain engagement
cards.takeaway: Across European interviews, recognition and time were the most frequently reported barriers to researchers’ science communication.
cards.finding: In interviews with 26 European stakeholders, lack of rewards or recognition and lack of time were each mentioned by 18 participants as barriers to researchers’ science communication. Lack of specialised training was mentioned by 12, indicating that workshop access alone sits within wider institutional constraints.
cards.context: European stakeholder interviews about science communication; study period not reported.
cards.qualityReason: The extract reports interview frequencies and categorised barriers, but does not describe sampling, recruitment, or analysis procedures.
cards.limitation: Interview mentions indicate perceived barriers, not their causal importance or whether changing them increases communication activity.
cards.connection: A free workshop might address training needs, but participation and follow-through may still depend on recognition and protected time.
cards.transferCaution: The evidence concerns researchers’ communication engagement across Europe, not science communicators’ responses to design-thinking workshops.
cards.discussionQuestion: Which institutional constraints would remain after a workshop removed direct financial cost?

cards.title: Trust Supported Contribution In Co-Design
cards.takeaway: Health-care participants described trust and relationships as conditions that enabled contribution and ownership in an open-ended process.
cards.finding: In interviews with all co-design participants in a health-care collective-leadership intervention, increased trust and stronger relationships were linked to teamwork, psychological safety and contribution. The process produced a self-facilitated training toolkit, but its intervention outcomes were still under evaluation.
cards.context: Health-care teams participating in collective-leadership co-design; interviews conducted March–August 2018, with ten interviews reported.
cards.qualityReason: Uses interviews with all participants and identifies themes, while relying on reported experience rather than outcome measurement.
cards.limitation: The extract does not show that trust caused better performance or that the resulting toolkit improved patient, team or organisational outcomes.
cards.connection: A workshop may generate richer communication ideas when participants feel able to question assumptions and contribute across professional boundaries.
cards.transferCaution: Health-care teams have different hierarchies, risks and organisational relationships from science-communication communities or workshop groups.
cards.discussionQuestion: What would make participants feel safe enough to challenge established assumptions about communicating science?

cards.qualityReason: Reports qualitative interviews with project members alongside documented researcher reflections.
cards.limitation: The extract identifies themes but does not show their prevalence, relative importance, or whether any response overcame them.
cards.connection: These barriers may expose why a free workshop still fails to engage people facing distrust, limited capacity, unequal power, or competing expectations.
cards.transferCaution: The setting was long-term participatory research with First Nation communities, not a one-off workshop for science communicators.
cards.discussionQuestion: Which workshop assumptions might conflict with participants’ safety, readiness, resources, or expectations?

cards.takeaway: Researchers rated design-thinking activities as useful for their project, especially empathy observation, but measures were self-reported.

cards.title: Dialogue Can Feel Like Unrewarded Work
cards.takeaway: Early-career scientists described public dialogue as time-consuming, outside their role, and sometimes lacking visible professional or research benefits.
cards.finding: Interviews with 19 early-career scientists in Japan identified reluctance toward science cafés because participation was troublesome or time-consuming, outside their work, offered no perceived benefit, involved pressure to represent science appropriately, and created apprehension about dialogue with the public.
cards.context: Early-career scientists who had participated in science cafés in Japan; study period not reported.
cards.qualityReason: Interview study identifies participant-reported barriers and gives the sample size and setting.
cards.limitation: Participants had already taken part in science cafés; findings describe perceived reluctance factors, not workshop attendance or broader prevalence.
cards.connection: A design thinking workshop may be judged by whether participants can see relevance and benefits for their existing communication work.
cards.transferCaution: Science café participation differs from professional science communication and from attending a free workshop.

cards.title: Communication Activity Rose After Training
cards.takeaway: Former course participants reported more frequent communication with nonexperts after training, alongside substantially higher retrospective confidence.
cards.finding: In a 2020 retrospective survey of 167 respondents who had completed the Art of Science Communication course between 2015 and 2020, the share reporting occasional or frequent communication with nonexpert audiences rose from 51% (86 respondents) before the course to 77% (128) afterward.
cards.context: Art of Science Communication alumni; course participation occurred from 2015–2020, with retrospective survey data collected in 2020.
cards.qualityReason: Reports explicit denominators and statistical comparisons from course alumni, supplemented by qualitative responses.
cards.limitation: The 37% response rate and retrospective before-after design permit selection and recall bias; increased activity cannot be attributed solely to the course.
cards.connection: A free workshop might lower access barriers and encourage later communication activity if participants perceive the methods as usable.
cards.transferCaution: The participants were scientists in a specific course, not necessarily professional science communicators, and the course was not identified as design thinking.

cards.title: Promotion systems undervalue public engagement
cards.takeaway: Workshop participants and academic stakeholders linked limited public engagement to time pressure, weak career rewards, and absent implementation infrastructure.
cards.finding: A National Academies workshop summary reports that life-science participants identified limited time, money, training, and professional cultures that undervalue public engagement. They also cited promotion and tenure criteria as barriers, while noting that NSF’s Broader Impacts criterion lacked infrastructure to help grantees maximise impacts.
cards.context: US National Academies workshop on life-science communication infrastructure; date not reported in the extract.
cards.qualityReason: The source synthesises workshop discussions from named stakeholders, but the extract gives no systematic sampling or outcome evaluation.
cards.limitation: Reported concerns and institutional examples do not demonstrate that changing promotion criteria or infrastructure causes better public engagement.
cards.connection: A workshop may be more useful when connected to institutional infrastructure, rather than treating communication capability as an individual deficit.
cards.transferCaution: The setting is US life-science academia and the evidence concerns public engagement, not science communicators’ professional development.
cards.discussionQuestion: What dependencies would need to change for workshop learning to survive existing promotion and workload systems?

cards.limitation: The extract does not quantify harms or demonstrate how particular adaptations changed participation or outcomes.
cards.connection: A free workshop could still exclude people if its formats, assumptions or institutional associations signal that some voices are less welcome.
cards.transferCaution: The paper concerns underserved communities and participatory design research; science communicators may face different histories, risks and power relations.
cards.discussionQuestion: Which workshop conventions might unintentionally signal expertise, gatekeeping or institutional power to prospective participants?

cards.context: Science communication trainers interviewed; setting and interview period not reported.

cards.title: Professional development lacks formal structure
cards.takeaway: Science communication practitioners reportedly have training options but little systematic or accredited professional development outside universities.
cards.finding: A UK forum report describes science communication practitioners as having no systematic formal professional development. cards.connection: A free design-thinking workshop might fill a short-term skills gap, while also exposing a broader need for coherent professional-development pathways.
cards.transferCaution: The report discusses science communication practitioners generally and does not specifically assess design thinking or free workshops.

cards.title: Extractive Climate Research Dominates

cards.finding: A global systematic review of climate field studies accessing Indigenous knowledge found that 87% used an extractive model, with minimal community participation or decision-making authority. cards.finding: A review of co-design research in health education found many methods supporting stakeholder collaboration, but no clear way to evaluate outcomes. Most studies focused on generating products, while one in three reported process enhancement as an outcome; co-design was also described as time-consuming and loosely defined.
cards.context: Review of research using co-design methods in health education; publication date and number of included studies are not reported in the extract.
cards.qualityReason: Synthesises reviewed literature and identifies evaluation patterns, but the supplied extract omits search methods and review scope.
cards.limitation: The review concerns health education, so it cannot establish which workshop outcomes or measures apply to science communication.
cards.connection: A free workshop may need explicit outcome definitions because participation, artefacts and longer-term practice change are different results.
cards.transferCaution: Health-education co-design literature may use different goals, stakeholders and evaluation standards from science-communication workshops.
cards.discussionQuestion: Which outcomes would distinguish a valuable science-communication workshop from one that merely produces attractive ideas?

cards.title: Participation Often Goes Unevaluated
cards.takeaway: Literature frequently claimed participatory approaches without demonstrating collaboration in framing, methods, language, or dissemination.
cards.finding: A review of literature on research with Indigenous communities found that many publications stated a participatory approach but did not clearly demonstrate collaboration in framing questions, choosing methods, or selecting language and dissemination modes. Clear evaluations of whether participation was effectively achieved were also seldom shared.
cards.context: Review of literature on research with Indigenous communities; place and study period are not reported in the extract.
cards.qualityReason: Synthesises academic literature and explicitly identifies missing evidence about participation and its evaluation.
cards.limitation: The extract does not provide the number of publications reviewed or assess the quality of individual studies.
cards.connection: This suggests that a workshop’s participatory label may conceal weak involvement unless collaboration and outcomes are documented beyond attendance or satisfaction.
cards.transferCaution: The evidence addresses Indigenous research literature, not training evaluation or science-communication workshops.
cards.discussionQuestion: How would a workshop document meaningful influence rather than simply participation claims?

stations.title: Meaning Meets Missing Time
stations.story: Communicators value connection and social impact, yet limited time, resources, uncertain rewards, and dialogue pressures can make participation feel costly.
stations.question: When does a workshop feel worth joining amid competing duties and uncertain professional recognition?
stations.illustration: A scientist balances a small glowing conversation circle against a heavy clock and an empty funding jar.

stations.title: Promising Gains, Uncertain Reach
stations.story: Training evaluations commonly report improved confidence, skills, intentions, and activity, but self-selection, self-reporting, and limited follow-up complicate interpretation.
stations.question: Which changes persist, reach audiences, and exceed what participants might have done without training?
stations.illustration: A workshop seed grows two bright leaves while a gardener peers through a fogged window at its roots.

stations.title: Workshops Inside Unequal Systems
stations.story: Training sits within institutions where time, recognition, career incentives, infrastructure, and professional development remain fragmented or insufficient.
stations.question: What surrounding conditions would let workshop learning become recognised, supported communication practice?
stations.illustration: A small workshop table stands beneath a ceiling of clocks, locked doors, and one open support beam.

stations.title: Co-Design Needs Trust And Proof
stations.story: Co-design examples suggest trust and short formats can support contribution, while unclear evaluation and participation risks leave benefits and harms unresolved.
stations.question: How might a workshop make trust, participation, workload, and outcomes visible without treating attendance as success?
stations.illustration: Three people assemble a bridge from small wooden pieces while one loose plank rests beside an unwritten measuring tape.

stations.title: Participation Or Borrowed Permission
stations.story: Participatory work can share authority, yet distrust, power differences, predetermined agendas, and weak evaluation risk turning inclusion into performance.
stations.question: Who sets the agenda, controls decisions, and defines meaningful participation before a workshop begins?
stations.illustration: Two people approach a round table, but a third person holds the table’s steering wheel beneath it.

stations.title: Design Activities Show Openings
stations.story: Design-based activities have been perceived as useful and linked with outreach or teaching gains, but evidence does not establish effects for free workshops.
stations.question: Which design activities could address communicators’ goals, and what evidence would distinguish usefulness from enthusiasm?
